section.heading: 8.4 Hyperplanes
section.paragraph: Hyperplanes play a special role in the geometry of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ because they divide the space into two disjoint pieces, just as a plane separates $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ into two parts and a line cuts through $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ . The key to working with hyperplanes is to use simple implicit descriptions, rather than the explicit or parametric representations of lines and planes used in the earlier work with affine sets.1

An implicit equation of a line in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ has the form $$ax + by = d$$ . An implicit equation of a plane in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ has the form $$ax + by + cz = d$$ . Both equations describe the line or plane as the set of all points at which a linear expression (also called a linear functional) has a fixed value, $$d$$ .﻿

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: A linear functional on $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is a linear transformation $$f$$ from $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ into $$\mathbb{R}$$ . For each scalar $$d$$ in $$\mathbb{R}$$ , the symbol $$[\textit{f} \text{:} d]$$ denotes the set of all $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ at which the value of $$f$$ is $$d$$ . That is,
The zero functional is the transformation such that $$f(\textbf{x}) = 0$$ for all $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . All other linear functionals on $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ are said to be nonzero.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: In $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ , the line $$x - 4y = 13$$ is a hyperplane in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ , and it is the set of points at which the linear functional $$f(x,y) = x - 4y$$ has the value $$13$$ . That is, the line is the set $$\lbrack f:13\rbrack$$ .﻿

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: In $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ , the plane $$5x - 2y + 3z = 21$$ is a hyperplane, the set of points at which the linear functional $$g(x,y,z) = 5x - 2y + 3z$$ has the value $$21$$ . This hyperplane is the set $$\lbrack g:21\rbrack$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: If $$f$$ is a linear functional on $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , then the standard matrix of this linear transformation $$f$$ is a $$1 \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ , say $$A = \begin{bmatrix} a_{1} & a_{2} & \cdots & a_{n} \end{bmatrix}$$ . So
$$\left[\right. f : 0 \left]\right. \text{is} \text{the} \text{same} \text{as} \left{\right. \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{n} : A \mathbf{x} = 0 \left.\right} = \text{Nul} A$$

If $$f$$ is a nonzero functional, then rank $$A = 1$$ , and dim $$\text{Nul} A = n - 1$$ , by the Rank Theorem.2 Thus, the subspace $$\lbrack f:0\rbrack$$ has dimension $$n - 1$$ and so is a hyperplane. Also, if $$d$$ is any number in $$\mathbb{R}$$ , then
$$\left[\right. f : d \left]\right. & \text{is} \text{the} \text{same} \text{as} & \left{\right. \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{n} : A \mathbf{x} = d \left.\right}$$

Recall from Theorem 6 in Section 1.5 that the set of solutions of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ is obtained by translating the solution set of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0},$$ using any particular solution $$\textbf{p}$$ of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ . When $$A$$ is the standard matrix of the transformation $$f$$ , this theorem says that
$$\left[\right. f : d \left]\right. = \left[\right. f : 0 \left]\right. + \mathbf{p} & \text{for} \text{any} \mathbf{p} \text{in} \left[\right. f : d \left]\right.$$
Thus the sets $$\lbrack f:d\rbrack$$ are hyperplanes parallel to $$\lbrack f:0\rbrack.$$ See Figure 1.

image.alt: A three dimensional graph shows two parallel hyperplanes on top of each other with a vector in between.

section.paragraph: When $$A$$ is a $$1 \times n$$ matrix, the equation $$A\textbf{x} = d$$ may be written with an inner product $$\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x}$$ , using $$\textbf{n}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ with the same entries as $$A$$ . Thus, from (2),
$$\left[\right. f : d \left]\right. & \text{is} \text{the} \text{same} \text{as} & \left{\right. \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{n} : \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} = d \left.\right}$$

Then $$\lbrack f:0\rbrack = \left\{ \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}:\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} = 0 \right\}$$ , which shows that $$\lbrack f:0\rbrack$$ is the orthogonal complement of the subspace spanned by $$\textbf{n}.$$ In the terminology of calculus and geometry for $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ , $$\textbf{n}$$ is called a normal vector to $$\lbrack f:0\rbrack$$ . (A “normal” vector in this sense need not have unit length.) Also, $$\textbf{n}$$ is said to be normal to each parallel hyperplane $$\lbrack f:d\rbrack$$ , even though $$\textbf{n} \cdot \textbf{x}$$ is not zero when $$d \neq 0$$ .﻿

Another name for $$\lbrack f:d\rbrack$$ is a level set of $$f$$ , and $$\textbf{n}$$ is sometimes called the gradient of $$f$$ when $$f(\textbf{x}) = \textbf{n} \cdot \textbf{x}$$ for each $$\textbf{x}$$ .﻿

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Let $$\textbf{n} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$\mathbf{v} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ {- 6} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and let $$H = \left\{ \textbf{x}:\textbf{n} \cdot \textbf{x} = 12 \right\}$$ , so $$H = \left\lbrack f:12 \right\rbrack$$ , where $$f(x,y) = 3x + 4y$$ . Thus $$H$$ is the line $$3x + 4y = 12$$ . Find an implicit description of the parallel hyperplane (line) $$H_{1} = H + \textbf{v.}$$ ﻿
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: First, find a point $$\textbf{p}$$ in $$H_{1}$$ . To do this, find a point in $$H$$ and add $$\textbf{v}$$ to it. For instance, $$\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$$ is in $$H,$$ so $$\textbf{p} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ {- 6} \end{array} \right\rbrack + \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ {- 3} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ is in $$H_{1}$$ . Now, compute $$\textbf{n} \cdot \textbf{p} = - 9$$ . This shows that $$H_{1} = \left\lbrack f: - 9 \right\rbrack$$ . See Figure 2, which also shows the subspace $$H_{0} = \left\{ \textbf{x}:\textbf{n} \cdot \textbf{x} = 0 \right\}$$ .﻿

image.alt: A graph shows three parallel straight lines along with two vectors.

section.paragraph: The next three examples show connections between implicit and explicit descriptions of hyperplanes. Example 4 begins with an implicit form.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: In $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ , give an explicit description of the line $$x - 4y = 13$$ in parametric vector form.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: This amounts to solving a nonhomogeneous equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ , where $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & {- 4} \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$\textbf{b}$$ is the number $$13$$ in $$\mathbb{R}$$ . Write $$x = 13 + 4y$$ , where $$y$$ is a free variable. In parametric form, the solution is

$$\mathbf{x} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}x \\ y\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}\begin{matrix}13 + 4 y \\ y\end{matrix}\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}13 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. + y \left[\right. \begin{matrix}4 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \mathbf{p} + y \mathbf{q} , & y \in \mathbb{R}$$

section.paragraph: Converting an explicit description of a line into implicit form is more involved. The basic idea is to construct $$[f \text{:} 0]$$ and then find $$d$$ for $$\left\lbrack f \text{:} d \right\rbrack$$ .﻿

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Let $$\textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ , and let $$L_{1}$$ be the line through $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ . Find a linear functional $$f$$ and a constant $$d$$ such that $$L_{1} = {[f \text{:} d]}$$ .﻿
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The line $$L_{1}$$ is parallel to the translated line $$L_{0}$$ through $$\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ and the origin. The defining equation for $$L_{0}$$ has the form

$$\left[\right. \begin{matrix}a & b\end{matrix} \left]\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}x \\ y\end{matrix} \left]\right. = 0 & \text{or} & n \cdot x = 0 , & \text{where} & n = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}a \\ b\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$
Since $$\textbf{n}$$ is orthogonal to the subspace $$L_{0}$$ , which contains $$\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ , compute
$$\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ - 2 \end{bmatrix}$$
and solve
$$\begin{bmatrix} a & b \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ - 2 \end{bmatrix} = 0$$

By inspection, a solution is $${[\begin{matrix} a & b \end{matrix}]} = {[\begin{matrix} 2 & 5 \end{matrix}]}$$ . Let $$f(x,y) = 2x + 5y$$ . From (5), $$L_{0} = \lbrack f:0\rbrack$$ , and $$L_{1} = \lbrack f:d\rbrack$$ for some $$d$$ . Since $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ is on line $$L_{1}$$ , $$d = f\left( \textbf{v}_{1} \right) = 2(1) + 5(2) = 12$$ . Thus, the equation for $$L_{1}$$ is $$2x + 5y = 12$$ . As a check, note that $$f\left( \textbf{v}_{2} \right) = f(6,0) = 2(6) + 5(0) = 12$$ , so $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ is on $$L_{1}$$ , too.

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Let $$\textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ {- 1} \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}$$ , and $$\textbf{v}_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$$ . Find an implicit description $$\left\lbrack {{f} \text{:} d} \right\rbrack$$ of the plane $$H_{1}$$ that passes through $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{v}_{3}$$ .﻿
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: $$H_{1}$$ is parallel to a plane $$H_{0}$$ through the origin that contains the translated points
$$v_{2} - v_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 \\ - 2 \\ 3\end{matrix} \left]\right. & \text{and} & v_{3} - v_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$

Since these two points are linearly independent, $$H_{0} = \text{Span} \left\{ \textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{3} - \textbf{v}_{1} \right\}$$ . Let $$\textbf{n} = \begin{bmatrix} a \\ b \\ c \end{bmatrix}$$ be the normal to $$H_{0}$$ . Then $$\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{3} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ are each orthogonal to $$\textbf{n}$$ . That is, $$(\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1}) \cdot \textbf{n} = 0$$ and $$\left( \textbf{v}_{3} - \textbf{v}_{1} \right) \cdot \textbf{n} = 0$$ . These two equations form a system whose augmented matrix can be row reduced:

$$\left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & - 2 & 3\end{matrix} \left]\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{matrix} \left]\right. = 0 , & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}2 & 0 & 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{matrix} \left]\right. = 0 , & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & - 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1 & 0\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$

Row operations yield $$a = \left( - \frac{2}{4} \right)c$$ , $$b = \left( \frac{5}{4} \right)c$$ , with $$c$$ free. Set $$c = 4$$ , for instance. Then $$\textbf{n} = \begin{bmatrix} {- 2} \\ 5 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$H_{0} = [\textit{f} \text{:0]}$$ , where $$f\left( \textbf{x} \right) = - 2x_{1} + 5x_{2} + 4x_{3}$$ .﻿

The parallel hyperplane $$H_{1}$$ is $$\lbrack f:d\rbrack$$ . To find $$d$$ , use the fact that $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ is in $$H_{1}$$ , and compute $$d = f\left( \textbf{v}_{1} \right) = f(1,1,1) = - 2(1) + 5(1) + 4(1) = 7$$ . As a check, compute $$f\left( \textbf{v}_{2} \right) = f(2, - 1,4) = - 2(2) + 5( - 1) + 4(4) = 16 - 9 = 7$$ . Observe $$f(\textbf{v}_{3}) = 7$$ also.

section.paragraph: The procedure in Example 6 generalizes to higher dimensions. However, for the special case of $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ , one can also use the cross-product formula to compute $$\textbf{n}$$ , using a symbolic determinant as a mnemonic device:

$$n & = & \left(\right. \mathbf{v}_{2} - \mathbf{v}_{1} \left.\right) \times \left(\right. \mathbf{v}_{3} - \mathbf{v}_{1} \left.\right) & = & \left|\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 2 & i \\ - 2 & 0 & j \\ 3 & 1 & k\end{matrix} \left|\right. = \left|\right. \begin{matrix}- 2 & 0 \\ 3 & 1\end{matrix} \left|\right. \mathbf{i} - \left|\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{matrix} \left|\right. \mathbf{j} + \left|\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 2 \\ - 2 & 0\end{matrix} \left|\right. \mathbf{k} & = & - 2 \mathbf{i} + 5 \mathbf{j} + 4 \mathbf{k} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 2 \\ 5 \\ 4\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$
If only the formula for $$f$$ is needed, the cross-product calculation may be written as an ordinary determinant:

$$f \left(\right. x_{1} , x_{2} , x_{3} \left.\right) & = & \left|\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 2 & x_{1} \\ - 2 & 0 & x_{2} \\ 3 & 1 & x_{3}\end{matrix} \left|\right. = \left|\right. \begin{matrix}- 2 & 0 \\ 3 & 1\end{matrix} \left|\right. x_{1} - \left|\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{matrix} \left|\right. x_{2} + \left|\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 2 \\ - 2 & 0\end{matrix} \left|\right. x_{3} & = & - 2 x_{1} + 5 x_{2} + 4 x_{3}$$

So far, every hyperplane examined has been described as $$\lbrack f:d\rbrack$$ for some linear functional $$f$$ and some $$d$$ in $$\mathbb{R}$$ , or equivalently as $$\left\{ \textbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}:\textbf{n} \cdot \textbf{x} = d \right\}$$ for some $$\textbf{n}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . The following theorem shows that every hyperplane has these equivalent descriptions.

note.title: Theorem ﻿11﻿
note.heading: Theorem ﻿11﻿
note.paragraph: A subset $$H$$ of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is a hyperplane if and only if $$H = \lbrack f:d\rbrack$$ for some nonzero linear functional $$f$$ and some scalar $$d$$ in $$\mathbb{R}$$ . Thus, if $$H$$ is a hyperplane, there exist a nonzero vector $$\textbf{n}$$ and a real number $$d$$ such that $$H = \left\{ \textbf{x}:\textbf{n} \cdot \textbf{x} = d \right\}$$ .﻿

section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: Suppose that $$H$$ is a hyperplane, take $$\textbf{p} \in H$$ , and let $$H_{0} = H - \textbf{p}$$ . Then $$H_{0}$$ is an $$(n - 1)$$ -dimensional subspace. Next, take any point $$\textbf{y}$$ that is not in $$H_{0}$$ . By the Orthogonal Decomposition Theorem in Section 6.3,
$$\textbf{y} = \textbf{y}_{1} + \textbf{n}$$
where $$\textbf{y}_{1}$$ is a vector in $$H_{0}$$ and $$\textbf{n}$$ is orthogonal to every vector in $$H_{0}$$ . The function $$f$$ defined by
$$f \left(\right. \textbf{x} \left.\right) = \textbf{n} \cdot \textbf{x} \text{for} \textbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$$
is a linear functional, by properties of the inner product. Now, $$\lbrack f:0\rbrack$$ is a hyperplane that contains $$H_{0}$$ , by construction of $$\textbf{n}$$ . It follows that
$$H_{0} = \left[\right. f : 0 \left]\right.$$

[Argument: $$H_{0}$$ contains a basis $$S$$ of $$n - 1$$ vectors, and since $$S$$ is in the $$(n - 1)$$ -dimensional subspace $$\lbrack f:0\rbrack$$ , $$S$$ must also be a basis for $$\lbrack f:0\rbrack$$ , by the Basis Theorem.] Finally, let $$d = f\left( \textbf{p} \right) = \textbf{n} \cdot \textbf{p}$$ . Then, as in (3) shown earlier,
$$\left[\right. f : d \left]\right. = \left[\right. f : 0 \left]\right. + p = H_{0} + p = H$$
The converse statement that $$\lbrack f:d\rbrack$$ is a hyperplane follows from (1) and (3) above.

Many important applications of hyperplanes depend on the possibility of “separating” two sets by a hyperplane. Intuitively, this means that one of the sets is on one side of the hyperplane and the other set is on the other side. The following terminology and notation will help to make this idea more precise.

note.title: Topology in ℝn﻿: Terms and Facts
note.heading: Topology in ℝn﻿: Terms and Facts
note.paragraph: For any point $$\textbf{p}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ and any real $$\delta > 0$$ , the open ball $$B(\textbf{p},\delta)$$ with center $$\textbf{p}$$ and radius $$\delta$$ is given by

Given a set $$S$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , a point $$\textbf{p}$$ is an interior point of $$S$$ if there exists a $$\delta > 0$$ such that $$B\left( \textbf{p},\delta \right) \subseteq S$$ . If every open ball centered at $$\textbf{p}$$ intersects both $$S$$ and the complement of $$S$$ , then $$\textbf{p}$$ is called a boundary point of $$S$$ . A set is open if it contains none of its boundary points. (This is equivalent to saying that all of its points are interior points.) A set is closed if it contains all of its boundary points. (If $$S$$ contains some but not all of its boundary points, then $$S$$ is neither open nor closed.) A set $$S$$ is bounded if there exists a $$\delta > 0$$ such that $$S \subseteq B\left( \textbf{0},\delta \right)$$ . A set in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is compact if it is closed and bounded.
Theorem: The convex hull of an open set is open, and the convex hull of a compact set is compact. (The convex hull of a closed set need not be closed. See Exercise 33.)

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: Let

$$S = \text{conv} \begin{Bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} - 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} , \begin{bmatrix} - 2 \\ - 2 \end{bmatrix} , \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ - 2 \end{bmatrix} , \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \end{Bmatrix} , \textbf{p}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} - 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} , \text{and} \textbf{p}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} ,$$

as shown in Figure 3. Then $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ is an interior point since $$B\left( {\textbf{p}_{1},\frac{3}{4}} \right) \subseteq S$$ . The point $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ is a boundary point since every open ball centered at $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ intersects both $$S$$ and the complement of $$S$$ . The set $$S$$ is closed since it contains all its boundary points. The set $$S$$ is bounded since $$S \subseteq B\left( \textbf{0},3 \right)$$ . Thus $$S$$ is also compact.

image.alt: A graph shows a shaded square inside a dotted circle represented as set S.

figure.caption: Figure 3 The set S is closed and bounded

section.paragraph: Notation: If $$f$$ is a linear functional, then $$f(A) \leq d$$ means $$f(\textbf{x}) \leq d$$ for each $$\textbf{x} \in A$$ . Corresponding notations will be used when the inequalities are reversed or when they are strict.

note.title: ﻿Definition
note.heading: ﻿Definition
note.paragraph: The hyperplane $$H = \left[\right. f : d \left]\right.$$ separates two sets $$A$$ and $$B$$ if one of the following holds:
If in the conditions above all the weak inequalities are replaced by strict inequalities, then $$H$$ is said to strictly separate $$A$$ and $$B$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: Notice that strict separation requires that the two sets be disjoint, while mere separation does not. Indeed, if two circles in the plane are externally tangent, then their common tangent line separates them (but does not separate them strictly).
Although it is necessary that two sets be disjoint in order to strictly separate them, this condition is not sufficient, even for closed convex sets. For example, let

$$A = \left{\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}x \\ y\end{matrix} \left]\right. : x \geq \frac{1}{2} \text{and} \frac{1}{x} \leq y \leq 2 \left.\right} & \text{and} & B = \left{\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}x \\ y\end{matrix} \left]\right. : x \geq 0 \text{and} y = 0 \left.\right}$$

Then $$A$$ and $$B$$ are disjoint closed convex sets, but they cannot be strictly separated by a hyperplane (line in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ ). See Figure 4. Thus the problem of separating (or strictly separating) two sets by a hyperplane is more complex than it might at first appear.

image.alt: A graph shows disjoint closed convex sets with a straight line and a curve in the form of a boat.

section.paragraph: There are many interesting conditions on the sets $$A$$ and $$B$$ that imply the existence of a separating hyperplane, but the following two theorems are sufficient for this section. The proof of the first theorem requires quite a bit of preliminary material,3 but the second theorem follows easily from the first.

note.title: ﻿﻿Theorem ﻿12﻿
note.heading: ﻿﻿Theorem ﻿12﻿
note.paragraph: Suppose $$A$$ and $$B$$ are nonempty convex sets such that $$A$$ is compact and $$B$$ is closed. Then there exists a hyperplane $$H$$ that strictly separates $$A$$ and $$B$$ if and only if $$A \cap B = \varnothing$$ .﻿

note.title: ﻿﻿Theorem 13﻿
note.heading: ﻿﻿Theorem 13﻿
note.paragraph: Suppose $$A$$ and $$B$$ are nonempty compact sets. Then there exists a hyperplane that strictly separates $$A$$ and $$B$$ if and only if $$\text{(conv} A) \cap \text{(conv} B) = \varnothing$$ .﻿

section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: Suppose that $$\text{(conv} A) \cap \text{(conv} B) = \varnothing$$ . Since the convex hull of a compact set is compact, Theorem 12 ensures that there is a hyperplane $$H$$ that strictly separates $$\text{conv} A$$ and $$\text{conv} B$$ . Clearly, $$H$$ also strictly separates the smaller sets $$A$$ and $$B$$ .﻿

Conversely, suppose the hyperplane $$H = \lbrack f:d\rbrack$$ strictly separates $$A$$ and $$B$$ . Without loss of generality, assume that $$f(A) < d$$ and $$f(B) > d$$ . Let $$\textbf{x} = c_{1}\textbf{x}_{1} + \cdots + c_{k}\textbf{x}_{k}$$ be any convex combination of elements of $$A$$ . Then
$$f \left(\right. \textbf{x} \left.\right) = c_{1} f \left(\right. \textbf{x}_{1} \left.\right) + \hdots + c_{k} f \left(\right. \textbf{x}_{k} \left.\right) < c_{1} d + \hdots + c_{k} d = d$$

since $$c_{1} + \cdots + c_{k} = 1$$ . Thus $$f\left( \text{conv} A \right) < d$$ . Likewise, $$f\left( \text{conv} B \right) > d$$ , so $$H = \lbrack f:d\rbrack$$ strictly separates $$\text{conv} A$$ and $$\text{conv} B$$ . By Theorem 12, $$\text{conv} A$$ and $$\text{conv} B$$ must be disjoint.

example.heading: Example 8
example.paragraph: Let

$$\textbf{a}_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & \textbf{a}_{2} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & \textbf{a}_{3} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}3 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & \textbf{b}_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & \text{and} & \textbf{b}_{2} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}2 \\ - 1 \\ 5\end{matrix} \left]\right. ,$$

and let $$A = \{\textbf{a}_{1},\textbf{a}_{2},\textbf{a}_{3}\}$$ and $$B = \left\{ \textbf{b}_{1},\textbf{b}_{2} \right\}$$ . Show that the hyperplane $$H = \lbrack f:5\rbrack$$ , where $$f\left( x_{1},x_{2},x_{3} \right) = 2x_{1} - 3x_{2} + x_{3}$$ , does not separate $$A$$ and $$B$$ . Is there a hyperplane parallel to $$H$$ that does separate $$A$$ and $$B$$ ? Do the convex hulls of $$A$$ and $$B$$ intersect?
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Evaluate the linear functional $$f$$ at each of the points in $$A$$ and $$B$$ :

$$f \left(\right. a_{1} \left.\right) = 2 , & f \left(\right. a_{2} \left.\right) = - 11 , & f \left(\right. a_{3} \left.\right) = - 6 , & f \left(\right. b_{1} \left.\right) = 4 , & \text{and} & f \left(\right. b_{2} \left.\right) = 12$$

Since $$f(\textbf{b}_{1}) = 4$$ is less than $$5$$ and $$f(\textbf{b}_{2}) = 12$$ is greater than $$5$$ , points of $$B$$ lie on both sides of $$H = \lbrack f:5\rbrack$$ and so $$H$$ does not separate $$A$$ and $$B$$ .﻿
Since $$f(A) < 3$$ and $$f(B) > 3$$ , the parallel hyperplane $$\lbrack f:3\rbrack$$ strictly separates $$A$$ and $$B$$ . By Theorem 13, $$\text{(conv} A) \cap \text{(conv} B) = \varnothing$$ .﻿

Caution: If there were no hyperplane parallel to $$H$$ that strictly separated $$A$$ and $$B$$ , this would not necessarily imply that their convex hulls intersect. It might be that some other hyperplane not parallel to $$H$$ would strictly separate them.

note.title: Practice Problem
note.heading: Practice Problem
note.paragraph: Let $$\textbf{p}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$$ , $$\textbf{p}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} {- 1} \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ , $$\textbf{n}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ {- 2} \end{bmatrix}$$ , and $$\textbf{n}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} {- 2} \\ 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$$ ; let $$H_{1}$$ be the hyperplane (plane) in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ passing through the point $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ and having normal vector $$\textbf{n}_{1}$$ ; and let $$H_{2}$$ be the hyperplane passing through the point $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ and having normal vector $$\textbf{n}_{2}$$ . Give an explicit description of $$H_{1} \cap H_{2}$$ by a formula that shows how to generate all points in $$H_{1} \cap H_{2}$$ .﻿
